title: Coppola v. Kraushaar
lead: An alleged failure to deliver wedding gowns cannot support the claimed loss of a marriage and its expenses, but the pleaded contract claim still survives dismissal.

actors.name: Lorenzo Coppola
actors.role: Buyer alleging breach of a promise to deliver two gowns for his betrothed.

actors.name: Isidor Kraushaar
actors.role: Dress supplier sued for the failed delivery.

proceedings: The complaint was dismissed at trial before testimony.
The Appellate Division unanimously reversed with costs, allowing the contract claim to continue despite the remote damages theory.
limits: Facts are allegations accepted for pleading review. The appellate court awarded neither the demanded $500 nor a final $10 recovery; it did not find causation or permanent refusal to marry proved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Coppola orders gowns and explains the approaching wedding
sections.cue: What promises and notice did he allege?
paragraphs: Lorenzo Coppola alleged that on January 3, 1902, he ordered two gowns of a specified model from Isidor Kraushaar for his betrothed. He said the wedding was set for January 19 and explained that he was incurring substantial feast expenses. Kraushaar allegedly promised delivery by January 18 for $50 and received $10 immediately.

Coppola and his betrothed allegedly demanded the gowns on January 18 but did not receive them. His complaint attributed her breaking off the wedding to that failure and sought $500 for presents, wine, clothes and other expenditures said to have become useless. Neither gown was identified as the bridal gown. These were allegations, not facts proved through testimony.

sources.pinpoint: 92 N.Y.S. 437; transaction, notice and claimed losses

sections.title: The complaint is dismissed before any evidence is heard
sections.cue: Why were the claimed wedding losses too remote?
paragraphs: The trial court dismissed Coppola’s contract complaint before testimony began. On appeal, Justice Jenks agreed that the claimed $500 in wedding losses was unavailable. Such losses were neither an immediate and necessary consequence of the clothing breach nor shown to be within the parties’ contemplation at formation.

Notice of the wedding and deadline did not warn Kraushaar that the marriage would never occur without these dresses. A postponed wedding would not necessarily make the presents, wine and clothes useless. The asserted loss therefore depended on a permanent refusal to marry, which the supplier had not been specifically warned to contemplate. Under the foreseeability reasoning associated with Hadley, predictable disappointment did not by itself make that intervening choice chargeable to him.

sections.title: A defective damages demand does not defeat the pleaded breach
sections.cue: What claim remained despite the rejected consequential losses?
paragraphs: The action was against the supplier for the gown-delivery contract, not against Coppola’s betrothed for a broken marriage promise. Coppola had alleged an agreement, a $10 part payment and nonperformance. At the legal-sufficiency stage, those allegations and their reasonable implications could support evidence of a breach.

Nominal damages alone would prevent dismissal of an otherwise adequate claim. The alleged payment also required an inference of $10 actual loss, although no other actual loss was supported apart from the rejected remote expenses. An erroneous demand did not make the cause of action itself deficient. A treatise’s broader dispute about wholly executory consideration did not need resolution because Coppola had made an actual payment.

sources.pinpoint: 438–439; sufficiency, nominal damages and part payment

sections.title: The appellate court restores the claim without awarding the demanded sums
sections.cue: What did the unanimous result accomplish?
paragraphs: On March 3, 1905, the Appellate Division, Second Department, reversed with costs. Presiding Justice Hirschberg and Justices Woodward, Rich and Miller joined Jenks, with no separate writing.

The court did not award $500, enter a final $10 judgment or find the alleged events proved. It restored the contract claim even though any eventual recovery might be small. The limited damages analysis and the reversal of dismissal must therefore be recounted together.
